channel.title: HS2 Test 3 — Every SAQ
channel.description: Every short-answer question Test 3 can ask. She posts no question list (her words: "there is no such list"); her Module 3 learning checklist limits what she may ask, so every point on it has a track: her two named cases, the pedigree charts she says will be tested, her help-board topics, every question on her student-marked SAQ quiz, and the rest of the checklist. Then one track for the closed questions: the one-line facts her quiz keys ask that no written answer covers. Test 3 closes Mon 26 Oct · 37 questions · 65 min · about 30% of the marks written.
channel.itunes:author: HS2 SAQ Podcast

item.title: 01 · Start here: Test 3, and how this episode works
item.description: Every short-answer question Test 3 can ask. She posts no question list (her words: "there is no such list"); her Module 3 learning checklist limits what she may ask, so every point on it has a track: her two named cases, the pedigree charts she says will be tested, her help-board topics, every question on her student-marked SAQ quiz, and the rest of the checklist. Then one track for the closed questions: the one-line facts her quiz keys ask that no written answer covers.

item.title: 02 · Case L: Jack's noise-induced hearing loss
item.description: Jack works in a very noisy open-plan office and has listened to loud music for a long time to drown it out. He now has trouble hearing and understanding. Which parts of the ear are damaged, and where are they? How does loud noise over time damage them, and how does that lead to deafness? What kind of deafness is this, and how does it compare with the other kind?

item.title: 03 · Case L, question 5: otosclerosis
item.description: A CT scan of Jack's ears shows no signs of otosclerosis. What kind of deafness would otosclerosis have caused, what specific structure of the ear is damaged by that condition, in what part of the ear is this structure(s) found and how does this damage impact hearing?

item.title: 04 · Case 11: Pania's milk coming in
item.description: Pania is 2 days postpartum and her milk is just 'coming in'. Two hormones are involved in the production and release of breast milk: for each, say where it is made or secreted from, what stimulates it, and its function. Describe the structure of the mammary gland and the path milk takes out of the breast. What type of gland is it, and what happens to the breasts in pregnancy as progesterone rises?

item.title: 05 · Case 11, question 5: the hormone tick table
item.description: Complete the following table about the roles of hormones in breast development, milk production and release by ticking the appropriate boxes (progesterone, oestrogen, prolactin, oxytocin): stimulates growth of milk ducts and glands · increases blood flow to the breasts · stimulate development of the lobules and alveoli · stimulates milk production and the development of mammary glands · stimulates milk ejection by making the myoepithelial cells around the milk ducts contract, squeezing the milk towards the nipple.

item.title: 06 · Pedigree charts: she says they will be tested
item.description: Explain how you work out the mode of inheritance from a pedigree chart, how you assign genotypes, and how you find the chance of another affected child. Use an autosomal dominant family as your example: an affected father and an unaffected mother who have both affected and unaffected children.

item.title: 07 · Huntington's disease
item.description: Explain Huntington's disease as a genetic disease: its cause, how it damages the body, how it is inherited, and the chance of an affected child when one parent is Hh and the other is hh.

item.title: 08 · Glaucoma and cataracts
item.description: Explain glaucoma and cataracts: which part of the eye each one affects, what goes wrong, and how it affects vision.

item.title: 09 · The words of genetics
item.description: Find the terms by matching them to the correct definition: homozygous, heterozygous, allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, autosomal, X-linked, locus, chromosomes, genome, autosome, sex chromosome, variation, inheritance.

item.title: 10 · Using a Punnett square
item.description: Explain how a Punnett square is used to predict offspring. Work a Bb × Bb cross (brown eyes B dominant over blue b) and a codominant blood group cross (Iᴬi × Iᴮi).

item.title: 11 · Patterns of inheritance
item.description: Briefly explain these patterns of inheritance, with an example of each: codominance, incomplete dominance, polygenic inheritance and mitochondrial inheritance.

item.title: 12 · Multiple alleles, blood groups and X-linked genes
item.description: Briefly explain multiple allele inheritance and sex-linked (X-linked) inheritance, using the right genetics terms.

item.title: 13 · DNA, chromosomes and mutations
item.description: Understand the structure and function of DNA and RNA (review from BN1), and define some ways genetic abnormalities occur, including mutation, genetic disease and aneuploidy.

item.title: 14 · Karyotypes and aneuploidy
item.description: What is a human karyotype and how many chromosomes does it show? What is aneuploidy? Give two examples and explain how aneuploidy arises.

item.title: 15 · Detecting and treating genetic disease
item.description: Explain some ways genetic abnormalities are detected, including genetic testing and fetal testing, and what genetic engineering and gene therapy are.

item.title: 16 · The three regions of the ear
item.description: What are the three regions of the ear? Describe their structures and functions.

item.title: 17 · How hearing happens
item.description: Discuss how hearing occurs in humans, from the sound wave arriving at the ear to the sound being perceived.

item.title: 18 · Static and dynamic equilibrium
item.description: What is the difference between static and dynamic equilibrium? How and where is each detected?

item.title: 19 · The three layers of the eye
item.description: What are the three layers (tunics) of the eye? Give their structures and functions.

item.title: 20 · The retina: rods, cones and colour blindness
item.description: What receptors are impacted by colour blindness? What are the receptors for light, where exactly are they found, and how do rods and cones differ?

item.title: 21 · Near vision: the three changes
item.description: What changes occur in the eye to allow near vision? How is this undone for distant vision?

item.title: 22 · Myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism
item.description: Explain how myopia, emmetropia and hyperopia differ and how each error is corrected. What is astigmatism?

item.title: 23 · Waves: light and sound
item.description: Explain amplitude, wavelength and frequency and how we experience each. Compare light and sound waves, and explain the difference between reflection and refraction of light.

item.title: 24 · Taste: the taste buds
item.description: Briefly describe the structure of the taste buds and discuss the physiology of taste sensation.

item.title: 25 · Smell: the olfactory epithelium
item.description: Briefly describe the structure of the olfactory epithelium and discuss the physiology of olfaction.

item.title: 26 · The male reproductive system: every structure and its job
item.description: Make sure you can label all the structures of the male reproductive system and state their functions.

item.title: 27 · Semen, sperm count, erection and ejaculation
item.description: Describe the composition of semen and normal sperm count in relation to sterility. (Reproductive 6) Describe the physiology of the male sexual response and relate it to erectile dysfunction. (Reproductive 5)

item.title: 28 · Making sperm and eggs
item.description: Describe the gamete production process in males and females. What hormone from the brain drives this?

item.title: 29 · The female reproductive system: every structure and its job
item.description: Make sure you can label all the structures of the female reproductive system and state their functions.

item.title: 30 · The ovarian and uterine cycles
item.description: Describe the phases of the ovarian and uterine cycles in the female and how the hormones link them.

item.title: 31 · Male versus female: the comparison table
item.description: Tabulate the differences between the male and female reproductive systems, looking at: the function of LH, the function of FSH, the timing of gamete production, the size of the gametes, the timing of meiosis and the mobility of the gametes.

item.title: 32 · Hormonal control of sperm, and testosterone
item.description: Describe the hormonal control of spermatogenesis, and the physiological effects of testosterone during puberty. What are the functions of the sex hormone testosterone in males and females respectively? (her student-marked quiz, Q21)

item.title: 33 · Oestrogen, progesterone and the pill
item.description: Describe the physiological effects of oestrogen and progesterone, including the female secondary sex characteristics, and explain how the contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy.

item.title: 34 · The female sexual response, and four words
item.description: Describe the female sexual response: erection and orgasm, according to the effects of parasympathetic and sympathetic nerve impulses. (Reproductive 13, self-directed) Explain the terms menarche, menopause, amenorrhoea and dysmenorrhoea. (Reproductive 14)

item.title: 35 · The closed questions: facts no other track covers
item.description: Genetics: the chromosome conditions and fetal testing. The eye: the pupil, the image, and her conditions tables. The ear and sound: ototoxic drugs, pitch, sound shirts, Doppler. Fertilisation and early pregnancy (not on her checklist; asked in her quizzes).
